did_you_know.text: Did you know? David subdued the Philistines and took from them the "Metheg-ammah." The chapter presents this as one of David’s victories afterward.

Did you know? After striking down Moab, David measured its people with a rope and separated those who would be put to death from those who would be allowed to live. Later, Moab became subject to David and brought him tribute.
Did you know? David fought Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to restore his power at the Euphrates—a phrase indicating an attempt to establish his rule in that region.
Did you know? In the war against Hadadezer, David captured 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers. He crippled most of the chariots, leaving only 100 chariots.

Did you know? Aram Damascus came to help Hadadezer, but David struck down 22,000 of them. Afterward, David stationed officials in Aram Damascus, and Aram became subject to him and brought him tribute.
Did you know? David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer’s servants and brought them to Jerusalem. He also took a great deal of bronze from Hadadezer’s cities, Betah and Berothai.
Did you know? Toi, king of Hamath, sent his son Joram to David to congratulate him and ask about his well-being after hearing that David had defeated Hadadezer, Toi’s enemy.

Did you know? David did not use the spoils of war only for himself: he dedicated to the LORD the silver, gold, and bronze he had received from the nations he defeated, including Aram, Moab, Ammon, the Philistines, Amalek, and the spoils of Hadadezer.
Did you know? Alongside its account of his conquests, the chapter emphasizes David’s role as ruler: he reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people.

Did you know? The chapter includes an organized list of the officials in David’s kingdom: Joab was over the army, Jehoshaphat was the recorder, Zadok and Ahimelech were priests, and Seraiah was the secretary.
